run.question:
Alertmanager alert RequestErrorRate (severity warning) is firing for service otel-demo/frontend-proxy since 2026-11-17T06:16:01Z.
Investigate why this alert is firing.

report.summary: The RequestErrorRate alert on frontend-proxy is driven by the service's own ingress (server) spans carrying STATUS_CODE_ERROR: 16.3 error ingress spans in 05:56–06:26 and 2.2–4.4 error spans per 5-minute step across 05:51–06:21, while the paired client operation 'router frontend egress' records zero errors. The frontend-proxy access log shows what those errors are: HTTP 503 responses with flag UC and detail upstream_reset_before_response_started{connection_termination} against upstream cluster 'frontend' (plus one 0 DC downstream_remote_disconnect at 06:06:52). I found 20 such 503 lines from 05:51:54 through 06:19:40 on /, /api/products/*, /api/cart, /api/data and /api/recommendations, i.e. the frontend upstream closed connections before starting a response. The frontend workload itself is up and ready (pod frontend-675fd7b5c5-5vnt2 running since 05:35:04, Ready, 0 restarts, empty lastState; Deployment 1/1 available), reports 0 error spans, and its p95 span durations stayed in a narrow band (GET 165–237 ms, grpc ProductCatalogService/GetProduct 95–166 ms), so this is not a broad frontend outage and downstream product-catalog latency is stable. The exact trigger inside the frontend (e.g. keep-alive connection reaping) is not directly observable: the frontend container produced no stdout/stderr lines, Jaeger holds no traces after ~05:49:19, and no alert rule is loaded. The load-generator Deployment rollout at 06:06:51 is a change in the window but not the cause: the 503s predate it and its pod template is identical apart from a restartedAt annotation. The alert condition itself appears threshold-sensitive to a low, persistent 503 rate rather than to a new spike; no pre-incident metric baseline exists in Prometheus to prove an increase.

claims.text: frontend-proxy error signal: its ingress (server) spans carry STATUS_CODE_ERROR while its client operation 'router frontend egress' has zero errors. Per-5-minute ingress error counts over 05:51–06:21 were 0, 3.33, 4.44, 0, 3.33, 2.22, 2.22, and in the 30 minutes 05:56–06:26 there were 16.30 error ingress spans versus 34,350 UNSET ingress spans.

frontend-proxy's own access log records HTTP 503 with response flag UC and detail upstream_reset_before_response_started{connection_termination} against upstream cluster 'frontend' on /, /api/products/{productId}, /api/cart, /api/data and /api/recommendations, at 06:05:50, 06:07:53, 06:08:36 (x2), 06:10:42, 06:14:05, 06:14:22, 06:15:35, 06:17:27 and 06:19:40; the same window contains one '0 DC downstream_remote_disconnect' at 06:06:52 (11 of 11,307 lines lacked '- via_upstream').

The same 503 UC upstream_reset_before_response_started{connection_termination} responses against upstream cluster 'frontend' also occur earlier, at 05:51:54, 05:54:36 (x2), 05:56:02, 05:56:30 (x2), 05:57:15, 05:57:29, 06:00:05 and 06:00:06 — i.e. from the start of the frontend-proxy log buffer, well before the alert start of 06:16:01.

The 'frontend' upstream identified in those 503 lines is the frontend Service, whose only endpoint is pod frontend-675fd7b5c5-5vnt2 (100.96.2.93, port 8080); that pod is owned by ReplicaSet frontend-675fd7b5c5, which is owned by Deployment frontend.

The frontend and frontend-proxy pods are Ready and have zero restarts: frontend-675fd7b5c5-5vnt2 has been running since 05:35:04 with restartCount 0 and empty lastState, frontend-proxy-6b4d584985-4dlth likewise; Deployment frontend reports 1 replica, 1 ready, 1 available with MinimumReplicasAvailable.

The frontend service itself shows no error spans (0 for 'GET' and for all grpc.*/api-route operations in the 55-minute instant query), so its own telemetry does not show failed requests; the 503s are only visible from frontend-proxy's side.

Frontend latency and resources were steady in the observed steps: p95 for frontend span 'GET' was 165–237 ms and p95 for grpc.oteldemo.ProductCatalogService/GetProduct was 95–166 ms across 05:51–06:21; the frontend container's CFS throttle ratio was 0.25–0.31 and its working set 121–132 MB, against limits of CPU 100m and memory 200Mi.

The load-generator Deployment was rolled out at 06:06:51–06:06:52: new ReplicaSet load-generator-84895ffcd created its pod and scaled up 0→1, old ReplicaSet load-generator-57ffcd644 was scaled down 1→0 and its pod deleted. The new ReplicaSet's pod template carries kubectl.kubernetes.io/restartedAt=2026-11-17T06:06:51Z and has the same image (ghcr.io/open-telemetry/demo:2.1.3-load-generator) and identical env as the old one; the new pod shows 0 restarts.

The otel-demo flagd-config ConfigMap sets flag 'loadGeneratorFloodHomepage' to defaultVariant 'on' (variants off=0, on=100, description 'Flood the frontend with a large amount of requests'), while the other fault flags (adFailure, adHighCpu, adManualGc, cartFailure, emailMemoryLeak, imageSlowLoad, kafkaQueueProblems, paymentFailure, paymentUnreachable, productCatalogFailure, recommendationCacheFailure) default to 'off'.

Separate, steady background errors exist outside frontend-proxy: over the 55 minutes to 06:20:00, ERROR spans appear on flagd EventStream operations of fraud-detection (2.04), ad (2.04, span flagd.evaluation.v1.Service/EventStream) and recommendation (4.06, span /flagd.evaluation.v1.Service/EventStream), and those services' other ERROR series are 0; no evidence ties these stream errors to the frontend-proxy 503s.

Prometheus only returned data for the recent tail of the authorized window: a 24-hour query at 30-minute steps on frontend-proxy ingress returned just two points (at 05:55:52 and 06:25:52), so no pre-incident baseline exists in this source.

The sampled frontend-proxy spans available in Jaeger are from 05:49:17–05:49:19 and all carry http.status_code 200 with no error detail; no frontend-proxy or frontend trace was returned for 05:56–06:25.

The frontend server reaps idle HTTP keep-alive connections (e.g. Node/Next.js server keepAliveTimeout) at the moment Envoy reuses them, which Envoy reports as upstream_reset_before_response_started{connection_termination} and maps to the 503/ERROR ingress spans. Supporting observations are the exact response detail, the random spread of affected routes, and the otherwise healthy frontend (0 restarts, 0 error spans, flat p95); the keep-alive configuration itself could not be read.

The enabled fault flag 'loadGeneratorFloodHomepage' (defaultVariant 'on') adds request pressure that contributes to the frontend dropping connections. This remains unproven: frontend-proxy ingress volume was steady at roughly 2,900–3,140 spans per 5-minute step across the observed window, and there is no change history to show when the flag was enabled.

The frontend's low CPU limit (100m) and 25–31% CFS throttling may slow request handling enough to lose reused upstream connections at moments of contention. No evidence ties specific 503 timestamps to throttling spikes, and frontend p95 latency stayed flat, so this stays a candidate only.

The 06:06:51 load-generator rollout did not trigger the alert: the identical 503 UC upstream-reset responses were already being logged at 05:51:54, 05:54:36, 05:56:02, 05:57:15 and 06:00:05, and the new pod template has the same image and env as the previous ReplicaSet (only a restartedAt annotation differs).

A broad frontend outage or a slow product-catalog dependency does not explain the proxy errors: the frontend pod is Ready with 0 restarts and empty lastState, its ERROR span counts are 0, its p95 'GET' duration stayed at 165–237 ms, and its p95 ProductCatalogService/GetProduct duration at 95–166 ms.

gaps: The RequestErrorRate alert rule itself could not be read: list_prometheus_rules returned no data for rule_name=RequestErrorRate and for the unfiltered query, so the exact expression, window and threshold behind the reported 0.01111111111111111 value are unknown and the value could not be reproduced from a known formula.

Jaeger returned no traces for frontend-proxy or frontend in 05:56–06:25; the most recent frontend-proxy traces read are at 05:49:17–05:49:19, so the failing requests at the alert time cannot be inspected as traces.
The frontend container produced no stdout/stderr lines in the read window (0 lines read), so the application-side reason the frontend closes connections cannot be read from logs.

No change-history integration is available, so it cannot be determined when flagd-config's loadGeneratorFloodHomepage was set to 'on', nor whether the frontend Deployment template changed before the authorized window.

Prometheus series begin only around 05:46–05:55, so there is no pre-incident baseline; whether the frontend-proxy error rate rose compared with earlier periods cannot be established, and no latency trend should be inferred.

The 55-minute error query returned no ERROR series at all for cart, checkout, currency, email, image-provider, kafka, product-catalog, quote and shipping; those services are unknown, not verified error-free.
Queries for NetworkPolicy and ResourceQuota in otel-demo returned empty results, so no policy- or quota-based cause could be examined (an empty result only shows the query matched nothing).
Kube-state-metrics series for container restart/termination reasons were not among the available metrics; pod health was assessed from the pod objects' status and lastState instead.
next_steps: Read the RequestErrorRate alert rule from the Alertmanager/Prometheus rule files to learn its expression, window and threshold, and decide whether '> 0' is intentional or should carry a small non-zero threshold or a 'for:' duration.

Review the frontend server's HTTP keep-alive settings (Node/Next.js server.keepAliveTimeout) against the Envoy upstream idle timeout in frontend-proxy, and consider enabling retries for idempotent GET requests so a reaped idle connection does not surface as a 503.
Enable or collect frontend application logs (stdout or OTLP logs) to identify why the frontend closes connections before responding.
Verify whether the loadGeneratorFloodHomepage flag should be 'on' and check flagd flag-change history, since it is the only enabled fault-injection flag in flagd-config.
Evaluate whether the frontend's 100m CPU limit is appropriate given the observed 25–31% CFS throttling.
